what_it_is: An architecture where multiple specialized AI agents (e.g. researcher, writer, editor, media-buyer agents) coordinate with each other, often under a central orchestrator, to complete a complex workflow end to end.
why_marketers_care: Marketing teams are adopting MAS-style setups to run full campaign lifecycles (brief to launch, content generation, budget management) with specialized agents per function rather than one general-purpose agent, changing how martech stacks and workflows are architected.
example: Industry analysis cited independent (non-orchestrated) multi-agent systems amplifying errors roughly 17x versus centrally orchestrated MAS reducing that to about 4.4x, underscoring why orchestration design matters for marketing use.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Academic/technical term for decades, crossed into marketing-orchestration vocabulary through 2025-2026 as agentic marketing tooling matured
notes: MAS is a decades-old computer-science term; only its marketing-orchestration application is newly mainstream. Sourcing for the marketing angle is from marketing-agency/vendor blogs rather than a top-tier analyst report, hence medium confidence.

what_it_is: Server-to-server method (Meta Conversions API, and equivalents at Google, TikTok, Snap) for sending conversion event data directly from an advertiser's server to ad platforms, bypassing browser-based pixels and cookies.
why_marketers_care: As of 2026 CAPI is treated as table stakes, not an advanced optimization, because it restores signal lost to iOS privacy changes, ad blockers, and cookie restrictions, improving match rates and automated bidding accuracy.
example: Meta Conversions API paired with the Meta Pixel for deduplicated, more accurate event matching, as widely documented in 2026 implementation guides.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Meta CAPI launched 2020-2021 but became a baseline, non-optional requirement for advertisers through 2025-2026 as third-party signal loss deepened.
notes: Not newly coined, but its status shifted from optional to mandatory baseline within the Sept 2024-Sept 2026 window, which is why marketers now treat it as a must-know acronym.

what_it_is: Apple's successor to SKAdNetwork (SKAN), introduced at WWDC 2024 and substantially upgraded at WWDC 2025 (rolled out with iOS 18.4), for privacy-preserving mobile ad attribution.
why_marketers_care: Adds configurable attribution windows, native re-engagement attribution, and developer testing mode that SKAN lacked, directly changing how mobile UA marketers measure iOS campaigns; both frameworks run side by side in 2026.
example: Apple Search Ads added support for both SKAdNetwork and AdAttributionKit, per Singular's 2026 coverage.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Announced WWDC 2024, expanded WWDC 2025, real-world marketer discussion peaked through 2025-2026.
notes: Note per Kochava (2026): actual adoption of AAK is still negligible versus legacy SKAN as of mid-2026, despite heavy trade-press coverage.

expansion: Global Privacy Platform (renamed Global Privacy Protocol in early 2025)
term: GPP (Global Privacy Platform / Global Privacy Protocol)
what_it_is: IAB Tech Lab technical standard for transmitting consent, opt-out, and other privacy signals from sites/apps to ad tech vendors across multiple regulatory regimes (GDPR, US state laws, etc.) in one standardized string.
why_marketers_care: The IAB Tech Lab renamed it to Global Privacy Protocol in 2025 to clarify it's a standard, not a product; it now covers new US state sections (Maryland, Indiana, Kentucky, Rhode Island) and Google began supporting GPP National v2 from September 2025, making it operationally required for compliant programmatic buying.
example: Google Ad Manager's support for the IAB's Global Privacy Platform, documented by Google in its Ad Manager Help Center.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Standard developed 2022-2023, renamed and expanded through 2025 with new state sections effective Oct 2025-Jan 2026.

what_it_is: IAB Europe's updated consent-signaling standard, released 19 June 2025, which makes the 'Disclosed Vendors' section of the TC string mandatory to give technical proof (not just policy) that vendors were actually disclosed to users.
why_marketers_care: Migration deadline is 28 February 2026; after that date TC strings built on TCF 2.2 become technically invalid, and non-compliant ad requests default to Google's 'Limited Ads' mode, which can cut programmatic revenue by 40-60%.
example: Google Ads announced TCF 2.3 compliance becomes mandatory 28 Feb 2026 for all advertisers serving ads in Europe, per Dataslayer's 2026 briefing.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Released June 2025; enforcement and marketer urgency peak Sept 2025-Feb 2026.
notes: TCF itself is an older framework (since 2018); it is included here specifically because version 2.3 is the newly mainstream, deadline-driven update marketers must act on in this window.

what_it_is: A browser-level opt-out signal that automatically tells websites not to sell or share a visitor's personal information for targeted advertising, functioning as a universal opt-out mechanism.
why_marketers_care: 12 US states require GPC compliance by 1 January 2026 (California, Colorado, Connecticut, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Minnesota, Maryland, Delaware, Oregon, Texas); California's CPPA voted in August 2026 to formally name GPC inside CCPA regulations, and joint AG enforcement sweeps began September 2025.
example: Connecticut, California, and Colorado Attorneys General jointly sent enforcement letters in September 2025 to businesses not honoring GPC opt-out signals.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Signal specification existed since ~2021, but state-law mandates and enforcement activity making it a must-know marketer term concentrated in 2025-2026.

what_it_is: EU Digital Services Act (DSA) designation for online platforms with at least 45 million monthly active users in the EU, subject to the strictest transparency and advertising-disclosure obligations.
why_marketers_care: Marketers running campaigns on VLOPs (major social/search platforms) must meet DSA ad-transparency and targeting-disclosure rules; non-compliant companies risk fines up to 6% of global turnover (20% for repeat DMA gatekeeper violations).
example: DSA Article 46 codes of conduct for online advertising require platforms displaying ads and advertisers purchasing ads on VLOPs to participate in supply-chain transparency standards.
first_seen_or_mainstream: DSA VLOP obligations took effect August 2023, but marketer-facing ad-transparency codes of conduct and enforcement activity intensified through 2024-2025.

what_it_is: EU regulation setting mandatory rules for online platforms on content moderation, ad transparency, and targeted-advertising disclosure to keep users safe and markets fair.
why_marketers_care: Codes of conduct for online advertising (Article 46) require ad-supply-chain traceability; marketers targeting EU users must obey these rules or face fines, with several implementation deadlines landing in late 2025.
example: The DSA's advertising transparency requirements were discussed in an October 2025 EDPB public consultation response from ZAW (German advertising federation).
first_seen_or_mainstream: DSA entered force 2022-2023; ad-specific codes of conduct and marketer compliance activity concentrated 2024-2025.
notes: Legislation predates the window, but marketer-facing operational obligations and enforcement are newly mainstream in 2024-2025.

what_it_is: EU regulation that disciplines the economic power of designated 'gatekeeper' platforms (e.g. restricting self-preferencing and combining data across services without consent).
why_marketers_care: Gatekeeper obligations affect how marketers can target and measure on platforms like Google and Meta in the EU; repeat violations by gatekeepers can trigger fines up to 20% of global turnover, reshaping available targeting options.
example: Fasken's July 2025 overview explains how DMA gatekeeper rules interact with DSA advertising-transparency rules for EU-facing marketers.
first_seen_or_mainstream: DMA entered force 2022-2023; gatekeeper compliance changes affecting marketer workflows landed through 2024-2025.
notes: Legislation predates the window; included because gatekeeper-driven changes to targeting/consent options became operationally relevant to marketers in 2024-2025.

what_it_is: IAB Tech Lab standard that structures and transmits consumer data-deletion requests across the ad-tech supply chain, reducing manual handling of erasure requests between advertisers, platforms, and vendors.
why_marketers_care: Endorsed by the UK ICO in July 2025 and upgraded to V2 in October 2025 alongside GPP updates; gives marketers and their ad-tech partners a standardized, auditable way to honor deletion rights across complex programmatic supply chains.
example: IAB Tech Lab's Data Deletion Request Framework was formally recognized in the UK ICO's Online Tracking Strategy Update, per PR Newswire, July 2025.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Framework developed 2024-2025; ICO endorsement and V2 release in 2025 made it a live compliance topic.
notes: Still in public-comment/early-adoption stage as of late 2025; watch for broader uptake through 2026.

what_it_is: A standardized attention-measurement score (0-100), pioneered commercially by Adelaide, that synthesizes viewability, time-in-view, interaction, and contextual signals into one metric predicting ad efficacy; the IAB/MRC published joint Attention Measurement Guidelines in November 2025.
why_marketers_care: Google made AU a Custom Bidding signal in DV360 from mid-July 2026, and Amazon DSP launched Adelaide attention segments in June 2026 with a Quality Floor excluding MFA sites and low-AU placements — attention is moving from a research metric to an active bidding and buying lever.
example: Nielsen and Adelaide launched a unified reach-and-attention measurement view in 2025, per Nielsen's own newsroom release.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Adelaide's AU metric existed earlier, but IAB/MRC standardization (Nov 2025) and platform-level bidding integration (DV360, Amazon DSP) in 2026 made it newly mainstream.

what_it_is: Smart-TV technology that identifies exactly what content a viewer is watching (linear or streaming), generating viewing data used for CTV/TV ad targeting and measurement.
why_marketers_care: ACR data lets marketers de-duplicate CTV and linear TV exposure and target based on real viewing behavior, becoming a core input for 2025-2026 CTV measurement stacks as linear/streaming convergence accelerates.
example: Viant's advertiser guide explains how TV ACR data is used for cross-screen targeting and de-duplication.
first_seen_or_mainstream: ACR technology is not new (used since ~2015), but its role as a core, marketer-facing CTV measurement building block intensified through 2024-2026 as CTV ad spend grew.
notes: Technology predates the window; flagged because its marketer-facing prominence in CTV buying/measurement stacks is a 2024-2026 development.

what_it_is: Turkey's national database system (iys.org.tr) where businesses store and manage consumer consents for commercial electronic messages (SMS, email, calls); separate from and complementary to KVKK data-processing consent.
why_marketers_care: Turkish marketers must obtain İYS approval before sending commercial messages, on top of KVKK consent for processing personal data; since 31 March 2025 approval/rejection operations can only be performed through Official İYS Integrators, tightening compliance requirements for CRM and lifecycle marketing teams.
example: DSR Belgelendirme's 2026 guide documents current İYS application steps via MERSİS number and e-signature.
first_seen_or_mainstream: İYS system established under Turkey's e-commerce law (~2015-2020), but Integrator-only rule change (March 2025) and stricter 2026 penalty guidance made it newly urgent for marketers.
notes: System itself predates the window; included because operational rule changes (Integrator-only approvals, 2026 penalties) are newly relevant to Turkish marketers in this period.

what_it_is: A Google Ads Search-campaign feature (toggle) launched in 2025, bundling broad-match/keywordless query matching, AI-generated headline/description customization, and Final URL Expansion (FUE).
why_marketers_care: Rolling out fully by Q3 2025 and expanding into Dynamic Search Ads upgrades in 2026, AI Max delivers roughly 14% more conversions at similar CPA per Google's own data, making it a term PPC marketers must now know when planning Search budgets.
example: Google's own blog post 'Unlock next-level performance with AI Max for Search campaigns' documents the feature's rollout.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Announced/rolled out 2025 (previously private beta as 'Search Max'); expanded through 2026.
notes: Not a classic acronym (it's a product name), included as a short acronym-style term per task scope.

what_it_is: Low-quality websites engineered primarily to generate ad impressions via paid/clickbait traffic rather than to serve genuine editorial or utility value; no single industry-agreed definition exists.
why_marketers_care: Major buyers (e.g. GroupM) began excluding MFA sites from programmatic buys, and attention-scoring vendors (Adelaide) now build MFA-exclusion 'Quality Floors' directly into DSP segments (2026), making MFA avoidance a standard line item in media plans.
example: Digiday's oral history 'MFA should stand for made-for-arbitrage' traces the industry debate over the term's definition.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Term and industry crusade against MFA intensified from 2023 (GroupM ban) through 2024-2026 as ongoing definitional debates and buy-side exclusion lists matured.
notes: Origin of the term predates Sept 2024, but industry-wide operationalization (exclusion lists, quality floors) is concentrated in 2024-2026; borderline inclusion.

what_it_is: A browser-based, cookieless ad-attribution proposal (originally from Meta and Mozilla, now a W3C Private Advertising Technology Working Group draft) using differential privacy and secure aggregation to measure ad effectiveness without tracking individuals.
why_marketers_care: Represents one of several competing post-cookie measurement standards (alongside Google's Attribution Reporting API and Apple's Private Ads Measurement); the W3C's First Public Working Draft appeared in late 2025, signaling where cross-browser privacy-safe attribution standards may converge.
example: Mozilla's blog 'Privacy Preserving Attribution for Advertising' documents the original Meta/Mozilla proposal and its evolution into a W3C standard.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Proposed August 2024 (Mozilla/Meta); W3C draft progressed through 2025.
notes: Experimental; a Firefox implementation was tested and later removed, so real-world adoption is very low despite standards-track progress.

what_it_is: A generalized version of the retail media network model, applied to any company that owns first-party transaction data and customer attention beyond classic retailers: marketplaces, travel platforms, fintechs, delivery and rideshare apps. CMN lets these companies sell ad space to external brands based on their purchase or behavioral data.
why_marketers_care: Commerce media is expanding well past Amazon/Walmart-style retail media. Marketers now need to evaluate a much wider set of CMN partners (airlines, banks, delivery apps, ride-hailing) as new first-party-data ad inventory, and budgets are shifting there because of stronger ROAS versus open web display.
example: Forbes (April 2026): "Commerce Media Networks: The Next Frontier In Brand Advertising," describing CMNs as the generalization of RMNs to marketplaces, travel, delivery and financial platforms.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Term in circulation since roughly 2023 among adtech vendors, but reached broad marketer trade-press mainstream in 2025-2026 as McKinsey and eMarketer projected commerce media growing 20%+ CAGR through 2027.
notes: No em-dashes used. Distinguish from RMN/RMP already in dictionary; CMN is the broader umbrella term.

what_it_is: A commerce media network built by a bank, card network, payment platform, or fintech (e.g., Chase, Mastercard, PayPal) that monetizes its transaction-level, high-intent consumer data by selling advertising to brands.
why_marketers_care: FMNs give advertisers access to purchase-behavior data that is arguably richer than retailer data (income signals, cross-category spend). eMarketer projects FMN ad spend growing at roughly 107% CAGR from 2024-2026 in the US, making it a fast-emerging budget line for performance and brand marketers.
example: Mastercard Commerce Media launched October 2, 2025, citing reach across more than 160 billion transactions processed in 2024 and 500 million enrolled consumers (Digiday, eMarketer coverage).
first_seen_or_mainstream: Became a distinct, named category in trade press through 2025, with eMarketer publishing a dedicated "Financial Media Networks Explainer" and forecast in 2025.
notes: Directly answers the brief's request for commerce media acronyms beyond RMN/RMP.

what_it_is: A TikTok Shop live-commerce efficiency metric: total GMV (Gross Merchandise Value) generated per 1,000 livestream views. It is TikTok's equivalent of CPM but measured in sales output rather than ad cost.
why_marketers_care: GPM is the primary metric TikTok Shop sellers, creators, and agencies use to judge whether a LIVE session is actually converting, and TikTok's algorithm uses GPM signals to decide how much extra reach to give a livestream. It matters directly to any brand or agency running TikTok Shop LIVE selling, including in Turkiye/MEA markets.
example: TikTok Shop Seller Academy course "GPM Video Guide" and multiple TikTok Shop analytics guides cite benchmark ranges of roughly $80-250 GPM for most consumer categories, $300+ for beauty.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Became standard shorthand among TikTok Shop sellers and agencies through 2024-2025 as TikTok Shop LIVE commerce scaled in the US and Southeast Asia.
notes: TikTok Shop primary source (Seller Academy) confirms the metric exists but did not return the full definition text in the fetch; definition corroborated by two independent marketing sources.

what_it_is: A hybrid technical role blending RevOps, marketing ops, data engineering, and AI/prompt engineering to build and automate the systems (enrichment, outbound, lead routing, AI agents) that power a company's marketing and sales motion.
why_marketers_care: It signals a structural shift in B2B marketing organizations: technical GTM builders are now sitting alongside marketers, and marketing leaders are increasingly expected to hire or partner with this role to run AI-driven outbound and demand programs.
example: ZoomInfo ("What Is GTM Engineering? The Complete 2026 Guide") reports the title first appeared on Google Trends in April 2025, with GTM engineer job listings up roughly 205% between 2024 and 2025 and over 3,000 open LinkedIn roles by January 2026.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Emerged as a named role in 2024, went mainstream on LinkedIn/B2B hiring in 2025-2026.
notes: GTM itself is not a new acronym, but its use as a standalone role/title (GTM Engineer, GTM Engineering) is the newly mainstream unit here.

what_it_is: Organic content (LinkedIn posts, short-form video, behind-the-scenes clips) created by a company's own employees rather than its marketing team or paid influencers.
why_marketers_care: As UGC and influencer costs rise and audiences distrust polished brand content, marketers are formalizing employee advocacy/EGC programs; Forbes and multiple 2025 sources report EGC posts get several times more engagement and reach than branded posts.
example: Forbes Agency Council (Feb 2025), "The Hidden Power Of Employee-Generated Content," and multiple 2025 agency guides positioning EGC as a named content category alongside UGC.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Named and tracked as a distinct content category through 2025 trade press (Forbes, Metricool, DSMN8).
notes: CGC already exists in dictionary (likely Creator-Generated Content); EGC is distinct (employees, not creators).

what_it_is: A C-suite role that owns growth across the funnel (acquisition, conversion, retention) by blending marketing, product, and data functions, distinct from a CMO (brand/demand) or CRO (near-term revenue execution).
why_marketers_care: It reshapes marketing org charts: in many companies the CMO now reports into, or is replaced by, a CGO. Secondary sources citing a 2024 Gartner report state nearly 40% of Fortune 500 companies now have a CGO, up from about 15% two years earlier.
example: Cowen Partners, "All About Chief Growth Officers (CGOs)"; multiple 2025 executive-search articles document CGO appointments replacing or absorbing CMO scope.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Adoption accelerated markedly in 2024-2025 per the cited Gartner-sourced statistic.
notes: The 40%/15% Gartner figure is cited by secondary sources, not verified against a primary Gartner document; treat the precise numbers as reported-not-confirmed.

what_it_is: A unified operations function aligning marketing, sales, and customer success processes, data, and systems around shared revenue goals, replacing siloed MarketingOps/SalesOps/CS Ops teams.
why_marketers_care: RevOps has crossed from early-adopter to majority practice inside this window: secondary reporting citing 2025 data states 60.2% of companies now have an officially defined RevOps function, up from about 7% a year earlier, directly changing who marketing reports to and how marketing is measured.
example: Gartner's original 2021 prediction (75% of high-growth companies deploying RevOps by 2025/2026) is now widely cited as having materially played out, per multiple 2025 RevOps trend reports.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Term coined earlier (~2019-2021) but crossed into majority adoption and routine marketing-org vocabulary in 2024-2025.
notes: The 7%-to-60.2% adoption jump is reported by a secondary source (CETDIGIT/other blogs), not a primary Gartner or research-firm publication; flagged as reported-not-independently-confirmed.

what_it_is: EU directive requiring large companies to publish detailed, audited sustainability data, which in turn forces marketing/communications teams to back up any environmental or social claims with reportable evidence.
why_marketers_care: It is now a direct constraint on sustainability marketing and green claims: companies were expected to provide audit-ready data behind sustainability claims by end of 2025, and parallel EU green-claims enforcement (Green Claims Code, Greenwashing Directive) is escalating through 2025-2026, with fines up to 10% of turnover in the UK's parallel regime.
example: KPMG Ireland, "Top Sustainability Themes" briefings and multiple 2025 marketing-compliance guides tie CSRD directly to what brands can claim in advertising.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Enforcement and marketer-facing compliance deadlines landed through 2024-2025.
notes: Directive predates the window (adopted 2022) but its marketer-facing enforcement/compliance mainstreaming is squarely 2024-2026.

what_it_is: Amazon's privacy-safe data clean room where advertisers can analyze ad performance, build audience segments, and track cross-format customer journeys using pseudonymized Amazon signals plus their own data.
why_marketers_care: In 2025 Amazon opened AMC access to any advertiser running Sponsored Products, Sponsored Display, Sponsored Brands, or Sponsored TV, without requiring a DSP relationship or separate registration, sharply widening who can use clean-room measurement.
example: Adweek, "Any Seller Buying Sponsored Product Ads on Amazon Can Now Use Amazon's Clean Room" (2025).
first_seen_or_mainstream: AMC launched in 2021, but its access expansion to all advertisers in 2025 is what made it broadly mainstream for mid-market marketers.
notes: Product itself predates the window (2021); flagged because the acronym's mainstream reach among marketers is the 2025 access expansion, not the product launch.

what_it_is: An influencer with recognized authority/expertise in a category (originally medical/scientific, now beauty, tech, lifestyle), distinguished from a KOC (Key Opinion Consumer, an everyday user whose reviews read as authentic).
why_marketers_care: KOL/KOC terminology, long standard in Chinese social commerce (Xiaohongshu, Douyin), is now crossing into Western marketing vocabulary as TikTok Shop and cross-border commerce push agencies and brands outside China to adopt the same tiered creator strategy (KOL for reach, KOC for social proof), directly relevant to Turkiye/MEA marketers running cross-border TikTok Shop campaigns.
example: Reacherapp and multiple TikTok Shop growth guides explicitly frame "KOL" as the term Western brands scaling on TikTok Shop need to learn, importing it from the China playbook.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Long-established in China; crossover into mainstream Western/global marketer vocabulary accelerated in 2024-2025 alongside TikTok Shop growth.
notes: KOC already exists in the dictionary as "Key Opinion Consumer" (#257); KOL is its natural, closely related, and currently missing counterpart term.

what_it_is: Meta's ad product (rebranded publicly as "Collaborative Ads") that lets a brand and a retail/marketplace partner co-run Facebook/Instagram ads using the retailer's catalog and audience data, directing clicks to the retailer's product pages.
why_marketers_care: It is a direct bridge between social advertising and commerce/retail media, and its retailer network keeps expanding into quick-commerce and Turkiye/MEA-relevant marketplaces (Trendyol lists CPAS as one of its four core ad models). Meta highlighted CPAS as a growth driver for quick commerce in a December 2025 post.
example: Meta, "How Meta's Collaborative Ads Are Fueling Quick Commerce Boom In India" (about.fb.com, December 2025); Trendyol seller guides list CPAS (Facebook/Instagram) alongside product and store ads as a core advertising model.
first_seen_or_mainstream: Product launched earlier (around 2019-2020) but expanded materially into quick-commerce and additional regional marketplace partnerships in 2025.
notes: Product predates the window; included because its retailer footprint and marketer relevance (including Trendyol in the Turkiye market) expanded materially within 2024-2026.

what_it_is: A managed, modular, API-first technology and services model that lets a retailer stand up a full retail media business (ad serving, campaign management, reporting) without building it in-house.
why_marketers_care: As mid-size and regional retailers (relevant to Turkiye/MEA markets) try to launch their own retail media networks, RMaaS vendors are the fastest path to market; it is a category marketers evaluating new RMN partners will increasingly encounter.
example: Adhese, "Adhese launches Retail Media as a Service (RMaaS), strengthening leadership team with two key hires" (2025).
first_seen_or_mainstream: Emerged as a named vendor category in 2024-2025.
notes: Weakest-sourced item in this set: primarily documented via one vendor's own announcement (Adhese) plus a competing RMAAS.net product name; not yet confirmed as an industry-standard term via independent trade press (Digiday/eMarketer searches did not surface independent RMaaS coverage). Flag for editor to verify with a second independent source before publishing, or downgrade to notes-only.
